questions.q: What is the key distinction between asepsis and antisepsis in surgical practice?
options: Asepsis prevents microorganisms from reaching the surgical site, whereas antisepsis destroys microorganisms on living tissues using chemical agents
Asepsis uses boiling water on skin, whereas antisepsis uses steam under pressure on instruments
Asepsis applies only to postoperative dressings, whereas antisepsis applies only to theatre air filtration
Asepsis eliminates bacterial spores on skin, whereas antisepsis removes gross soil without killing bacteria
questions.explain: Asepsis encompasses all measures that keep microorganisms away from sterile fields and wounds (such as sterile drapes, gowns, and autoclaved instruments), whereas antisepsis uses chemical agents (antiseptics) on living skin or mucosa to kill or inhibit microbes.

open.q: Define the difference between asepsis and antisepsis in the operating theatre.
accept: Asepsis prevents microbial entry into sterile areas while antisepsis destroys microbes on living tissues
Asepsis excludes pathogens from the wound whereas antisepsis uses chemicals to reduce microbes on living tissue

questions.q: Which standard operating parameters are required for routine steam sterilization in a gravity-displacement autoclave?
options: 121 degrees Celsius at 15 psi (103 kPa) above atmospheric pressure for 15 to 20 minutes
100 degrees Celsius at atmospheric pressure for 30 minutes
160 degrees Celsius dry heat for 10 minutes
60 degrees Celsius ethylene oxide exposure for 5 minutes
questions.explain: Saturated steam under pressure at 121 degrees Celsius and 15 psi (103 kPa) for 15 to 20 minutes (or 134 degrees Celsius at 30 psi for 3 to 4 minutes in pre-vacuum autoclaves) destroys all microorganisms including heat-resistant bacterial spores.

open.q: State the standard temperature, pressure over atmospheric, and holding time used in a conventional surgical autoclave at 121 degrees Celsius.
accept: 121 degrees Celsius, 15 psi, for 15 to 20 minutes
121 C at 103 kPa for 15 minutes
15 psi at 121 degrees Celsius for 15-20 minutes

questions.q: Which biological indicator organism is used to validate the efficacy of steam autoclaving?
options: Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores
Bacillus atrophaeus spores
Staphylococcus aureus
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
questions.explain: Geobacillus stearothermophilus produces highly heat-resistant endospores, making it the gold-standard biological test for steam autoclaves. Bacillus atrophaeus (formerly B. subtilis var. niger) is used for dry heat and ethylene oxide sterilization.

open.q: Name the spore-forming bacterium used as the standard biological indicator for verifying steam autoclave sterilization.
accept: Geobacillus stearothermophilus
Bacillus stearothermophilus

questions.q: Which method is preferred for sterilizing heat-sensitive flexible endoscopes that cannot withstand steam autoclaving?
options: Immersion in 2% alkaline glutaraldehyde or orthophthalaldehyde (OPA)
Hot air oven at 160 degrees Celsius for 2 hours
Boiling in water for 20 minutes
Flaming over a spirit lamp
questions.explain: Heat-labile fibreoptic endoscopes are damaged by autoclaving and dry heat; high-level disinfection or cold chemical sterilization is achieved using 2% glutaraldehyde, orthophthalaldehyde, or peracetic acid.

open.q: Name a standard chemical agent used for cold high-level disinfection or sterilization of heat-sensitive flexible endoscopes.
accept: Glutaraldehyde
2% glutaraldehyde
Orthophthalaldehyde
Peracetic acid

questions.q: Why must a surgeon hold their hands above elbow level during and immediately after a surgical scrub?
options: So water runs downward from the cleaner fingertips toward the less clean elbows
To reduce venous pooling in the upper limbs before standing in theatre
To allow alcohol rub to evaporate more slowly from the palms
To prevent contact with the sterile gown collar
questions.explain: Keeping the hands higher than the elbows ensures gravity directs rinse water from the cleanest area (fingertips and hands) down toward the forearms and elbows, preventing contaminated water from flowing back onto the hands.

open.q: Why are the hands kept elevated over the elbows throughout a surgical hand scrub and rinse?
accept: To ensure water drains from the clean hands down toward the elbows
So gravity prevents contaminated water from running from the elbows back onto the hands

questions.q: Which antiseptic agent provides the longest residual antimicrobial activity on the skin after surgical hand scrubbing?
options: Chlorhexidine gluconate
70% isopropyl alcohol alone
Plain non-medicated soap
Normal saline
questions.explain: Chlorhexidine gluconate binds strongly to the stratum corneum, giving persistent residual bactericidal activity for several hours under surgical gloves. Alcohol acts fastest initially but has no residual effect once evaporated.

open.q: Which common surgical scrub antiseptic binds to skin proteins to provide prolonged residual antimicrobial protection under gloves?
accept: Chlorhexidine
Chlorhexidine gluconate

questions.q: Which regions of a sterile surgical gown are considered strictly sterile once the surgeon is gowned and gloved?
options: The front of the gown from mid-chest to the level of the sterile operating table, and the sleeves from 5 cm above the elbows to the cuffs
The entire gown front and back from collar to hem
Only the gloved hands and wrists below the cuffs
The shoulders, axillae, and entire back panel
questions.explain: In standard theatre practice, only the front of the gown from chest/axillary level down to the sterile field (table level) and the sleeves from 2 inches (5 cm) above the elbow to the cuff are considered sterile; the back, neck, axillae, and skirt below table level are unsterile.

open.q: Specify the anatomical boundaries of a surgical gown that are considered sterile during an operation.
accept: Front of the gown from chest to table level and sleeves from 5 cm above the elbows to the cuffs
Chest to sterile field level in front and sleeves from above the elbow to the cuff

questions.q: In what direction should antiseptic skin preparation be applied for a clean surgical incision?
options: From the planned incision line outward toward the periphery in concentric circles, never returning to the centre with the same swab
From the unsterile periphery inward toward the planned incision line
Back and forth vigorously across the umbilicus and groin before wiping the abdomen
Starting at the anus and moving upward toward the sterile abdominal field
questions.explain: Skin prep always moves from the cleanest zone (the intended incision site) outward toward the dirtier periphery so skin flora from surrounding areas are not dragged onto the incision. Contaminated areas like the umbilicus, stomas, or open wounds are prepped last.

open.q: Describe the proper direction of antiseptic application when preparing skin for a clean surgical incision.
accept: From the planned incision site outward toward the periphery without returning to the centre
Centre to periphery in concentric circles

questions.q: A surgical registrar prepares a patient's abdomen with alcoholic chlorhexidine and immediately activates monopolar diathermy before the solution has dried. What serious theatre complication is most likely to occur?
options: Operating theatre fire causing severe thermal burns to the patient
Acute anaphylaxis to chlorhexidine
Immediate coagulation necrosis of the rectus muscle from chemical toxicity
Failure of the diathermy return pad to detect impedance
questions.explain: Alcohol-based skin antiseptics are highly flammable; pooling in body hair, the umbilicus, or under drapes and igniting with a diathermy spark causes devastating operating theatre fires. Alcohol preps must dry completely before draping or diathermy use.

open.q: What major hazard occurs if monopolar diathermy is used before an alcohol-based skin preparation solution has completely evaporated?
accept: Operating theatre fire and patient burns
Ignition of alcohol vapour causing a surgical fire
Flash fire and thermal burns

questions.q: How is a scalpel loaded with a number 15 blade held when making a precise, controlled skin incision?
options: Like a pencil (pencil grip)
Like a dinner knife (fingertip grip)
Like a violin bow
In a closed palm fist
questions.explain: A small blade such as a No. 15 or No. 11 mounted on a No. 3 Bard-Parker handle is held like a pencil for fine, accurate dissection. A larger No. 10 or No. 20 blade is held like a dinner knife (fingertip grip) for long skin incisions.

open.q: Which grip is used to hold a scalpel fitted with a No. 15 blade for fine, accurate surgical dissection?
accept: Pencil grip
Like a pencil

questions.q: Which structural feature distinguishes a needle holder from a haemostatic artery forceps?
options: Short, stout, cross-hatched jaws often with a tungsten carbide insert and a central groove to prevent needle rotation
Long, slender blades with longitudinal serrations and curved tips
Sharp cutting edges along the inner blades
Two-by-three interlocking teeth at the tip of delicate tissue blades
questions.explain: Needle holders have short, strong, cross-hatched (or diamond-dusted) jaws designed to grip curved metal needles without slipping or twisting. Using artery forceps to hold needles damages the forceps' finer serrations and bends needles.

open.q: How do the jaws of a surgical needle holder differ structurally from those of a haemostatic artery forceps?
accept: Needle holder jaws are shorter, stouter, and cross-hatched rather than long with transverse serrations
Short stout jaws with cross-hatching

questions.q: Why should toothed dissecting forceps (such as Adson or Gillies toothed forceps) never be used to grasp bowel wall or blood vessels?
options: The sharp teeth crush and perforate delicate hollow viscera and vascular walls
Toothed forceps are magnetized and interfere with diathermy
The teeth cannot hold any tissue under tension
Toothed forceps are strictly single-use plastic instruments
questions.explain: Toothed forceps provide a secure grip on tough tissues like skin and fascia with minimal crushing force, whereas non-toothed (atraumatic, e.g., DeBakey) forceps must be used on bowel, blood vessels, nerves, and ureters to avoid perforation or thrombosis.

open.q: Which tissues are appropriately handled with toothed dissecting forceps, and which tissues require non-toothed atraumatic forceps?
accept: Skin and fascia with toothed forceps; bowel, vessels, and nerves with non-toothed forceps
Tough tissues like skin with toothed, delicate viscera and vessels with non-toothed

questions.q: Why do skin incisions placed along Langer's lines (relaxed skin tension lines) heal with superior cosmetic results?
options: They run parallel to the predominant orientation of dermal collagen fibres, minimizing wound tension
They sever cutaneous nerves cleanly so the scar remains painless
They lie directly over major subcutaneous veins for faster drainage
They eliminate the inflammatory phase of wound healing
questions.explain: Langer's lines correspond to the natural orientation of collagen bundles in the dermis; incisions made parallel to these lines experience minimal distraction force across the wound edges, reducing hypertrophic scarring and widening.

open.q: What is the anatomical basis for placing elective skin incisions parallel to Langer's lines?
accept: They align with dermal collagen fibre orientation, reducing tension across the healing wound
Parallel alignment with dermal collagen bundles minimizes wound edge tension

questions.q: Which of the following is a natural, absorbable, multifilament suture material?
options: Chromic catgut
Polypropylene (Prolene)
Polydioxanone (PDS)
Braided silk
questions.explain: Catgut (plain or chromic, derived from sheep intestinal submucosa or bovine serosa) is a natural twisted multifilament absorbable suture broken down by proteolytic enzymes. PDS is synthetic monofilament absorbable, while silk and polypropylene are non-absorbable.

open.q: Give an example of a natural absorbable suture material and state how it is degraded in the body.
accept: Catgut, degraded by proteolytic enzymes
Chromic catgut via enzymatic proteolysis

questions.q: Why are monofilament non-absorbable sutures (such as nylon or polypropylene) preferred over braided multifilament sutures in contaminated wounds?
options: Monofilament strands lack interstices that harbour bacteria and resist wicking of microorganisms
Monofilament sutures dissolve rapidly in pus within 48 hours
Braided sutures cannot be tied with a reef knot
Monofilament sutures release broad-spectrum antibiotics into the wound
questions.explain: Braided multifilament sutures have microscopic crevices between fibres where bacteria can hide from host neutrophils and macrophages, promoting persistent suture sinuses. Smooth monofilament sutures resist bacterial colonization.

open.q: Why do monofilament sutures carry a lower risk of persistent wound infection than braided multifilament sutures?
accept: They lack crevices between fibres that can harbour bacteria
Smooth surface prevents bacterial colonization and wicking

questions.q: Which suture needle point geometry is best suited for closing tough, dense tissue such as skin?
options: Reverse-cutting or conventional cutting needle
Taper-point (round-bodied) needle
Blunt-point needle
Spatula micro-point needle
questions.explain: Cutting needles have a triangular cross-section with sharp edges that slice cleanly through tough keratinized skin. Taper-point (round-bodied) needles push tissue fibres apart without cutting and are used for bowel, vessels, and peritoneum.

open.q: Which needle point type is used for suturing skin versus suturing bowel wall?
accept: Cutting needle for skin and taper-point round-bodied needle for bowel
Cutting for skin, round-bodied taper point for bowel

questions.q: What is the main structural advantage of a reverse-cutting needle over a conventional cutting needle?
options: Its cutting edge is on the outer convex curve, leaving a flat inner surface that reduces the risk of suture cut-out through tissue
It has no sharp edges and is used exclusively for liver parenchyma
It dissolves automatically after skin closure
It is mounted on a straight shaft that requires no needle holder
questions.explain: In a conventional cutting needle, the sharp cutting edge sits on the inner concave curve, which can slice through tissue toward the wound edge when the suture is tied. Placing the cutting edge on the outer convex curve (reverse-cutting) preserves tissue strength against pull-through.

open.q: Where is the third cutting edge located on a reverse-cutting needle, and why does this prevent suture cut-out?
accept: On the outer convex curvature, leaving a flat inner wall that resists tearing toward the wound edge
Outer convex curve so tension does not slice through tissue

questions.q: Which surgical knot is formed by reversing the direction of the second throw relative to the first throw so the ends lie flat and parallel?
options: Reef knot (square knot)
Granny knot
Slip knot
Aberdeen knot
questions.explain: A reef (square) knot consists of two opposing half-hitches (e.g., left-over-right followed by right-over-left) that lock securely under tension. Repeating two identical throws produces an insecure granny knot that tends to slip.

open.q: How does a reef knot differ in construction and security from a granny knot?
accept: A reef knot uses opposite throws that lock securely, whereas a granny knot repeats identical throws and slips easily
Opposite half-hitches in a reef knot versus identical half-hitches in a granny knot

questions.q: Why should skin edges be everted rather than inverted when placing interrupted skin sutures?
options: Wound contraction during healing flattens slightly everted edges into a level scar, whereas inverted edges cause depressed scars and poor epidermal apposition
Everted edges prevent dermal blood flow
Inverted edges accelerate keloid formation in all patients
Everted edges allow suture removal without cutting
questions.explain: Entering the skin at 90 degrees and taking a wider bite in the deeper dermis than the superficial epidermis everts the edges slightly; as the scar contracts over time, the wound flattens flush with surrounding skin.

open.q: Why is slight eversion of skin edges desired during wound closure?
accept: Normal scar contraction flattens everted edges into a level scar, whereas inversion produces a depressed scar
To compensate for scar contraction and ensure epidermal-to-epidermal alignment

questions.q: Which suturing technique is specifically designed to close dead space and achieve strong skin eversion in a single layered closure?
options: Vertical mattress suture (Donati suture)
Simple continuous running suture
Purse-string suture
Subcuticular running suture
questions.explain: The vertical mattress ('far-far, near-near') suture takes a deep wide bite to obliterate dead space and relieve tension, followed by a shallow narrow bite on the return pass to accurately align and evert the epidermal edges.

open.q: Name the interrupted suturing technique using a 'far-far, near-near' pass to obliterate dead space and evert skin edges.
accept: Vertical mattress suture
Donati suture

questions.q: When should non-absorbable interrupted skin sutures typically be removed from a clean facial incision?
options: 3 to 5 days postoperatively
10 to 14 days postoperatively
21 days postoperatively
24 hours postoperatively
questions.explain: Because the face has a rich blood supply, wounds gain adequate tensile strength rapidly and sutures are removed at 3 to 5 days to prevent permanent 'railroad track' suture marks. Trunk and limb sutures stay 7 to 10 days, and over joints 10 to 14 days.

open.q: What is the standard timeframe for removing skin sutures from the face compared to the anterior abdominal wall?
accept: 3 to 5 days for the face and 7 to 10 days for the abdomen
3-5 days on the face, 7-10 days on the abdomen

questions.q: How does bipolar diathermy differ from monopolar diathermy in its electrical circuit?
options: Current passes only between the two tips of the bipolar forceps, eliminating the need for a patient return plate
Current travels from the active electrode through the entire body to a dispersive pad on the thigh
Bipolar diathermy uses direct current rather than high-frequency alternating current
Bipolar diathermy cannot coagulate blood vessels smaller than 5 mm
questions.explain: In bipolar diathermy, one tine of the forceps is the active electrode and the other is the return electrode, confining current strictly to the grasped tissue. This makes it safe near nerves, digits, and in patients with cardiac pacemakers.

open.q: Why does bipolar diathermy not require a dispersive return electrode pad attached to the patient?
accept: Electrical current flows exclusively between the two tips of the forceps through the grasped tissue
Both the active and return electrodes are incorporated into the forceps tips

questions.q: During a circumcision using monopolar diathermy, severe tissue necrosis of the penis occurs even though the cutting power setting was low. What is the physical explanation?
options: High current density is funnelled through the narrow cross-sectional area of the penile base
The patient's return plate was placed too close to the pelvis
Monopolar diathermy stimulates parasympathetic vasodilation
The foreskin lacks any electrical resistance
questions.explain: Monopolar current returning toward the dispersive pad concentrates through narrow anatomical pedicles (such as the penis, digits, or testis on its cord), generating intense heat and thrombosis. Monopolar diathermy is contraindicated on end-artery pedicles.

open.q: Why is monopolar diathermy contraindicated during surgery on digits or the penis?
accept: Current funnels through the narrow pedicle, creating high current density and thermal necrosis
High current concentration in a narrow appendage causes vascular thrombosis and tissue necrosis

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a closed active suction surgical drain?
options: Redivac drain
Corrugated rubber drain
Penrose latex drain
Yeates capillary drain
questions.explain: Redivac and Jackson-Pratt drains are closed negative-pressure (suction) systems that actively evacuate fluid and collapse dead space while reducing retrograde bacterial entry. Corrugated, Penrose, and Yeates drains are open passive drains.

open.q: Classify Redivac and Penrose drains according to whether they are open or closed and active or passive.
accept: Redivac is a closed active suction drain; Penrose is an open passive drain
Redivac is closed active and Penrose is open passive

questions.q: What is the standard sequence for removing personal protective equipment (doffing) after a contaminated surgical procedure to avoid self-contamination?
options: Remove contaminated gloves first, perform hand hygiene, remove gown, then remove eye protection and mask
Remove surgical mask first, then pull gloves off using bare hands
Unfasten the gown neck ties with soiled gloves before removing gloves
Remove shoe covers first while still wearing bloody gloves
questions.explain: Gloves carry the heaviest microbial load and are removed first using glove-to-glove and skin-to-skin technique, followed by hand hygiene before touching clean ties on the gown, goggles, or mask.

open.q: Which item of surgical personal protective equipment should be removed first when doffing after an operation, and why?
accept: Gloves, because they are the most heavily contaminated item
Surgical gloves first to prevent contaminating clean skin or clothing
